title: Elder Nisabha: Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure, Those things so agreeable, Which delight the mind — With faith, I went forth, Putting…
content:
Elder Nisabha:

Having abandoned the five strands of sensual pleasure,
Those things so agreeable,
Which delight the mind —
With faith, I went forth,
Putting an end to suffering.

I do not delight in death,
I do not delight in life.
I await the time,
Mindful and clearly comprehending.

title: “Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind…
content: “Monks, before my enlightenment, while I was still a bodhisatta, not yet fully enlightened, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — regarding them, my mind becomes inflamed when they are present, and diminishes when they are future, not yet attained.’ Then, monks, I thought: ‘The five strands of sensual pleasure that this mind formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — regarding them, for my own benefit, I will dwell heedful, protecting my mind with mindfulness.’ Therefore, monks, regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure that your minds formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — your minds become inflamed when they are present, and diminish when they are future, not yet attained. Therefore, monks, regarding the five strands of sensual pleasure that your minds formerly experienced — now past, ceased, changed — for your own benefit, dwell heedful, protecting your minds with mindfulness.”

title: “Monks, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon your desire for it. And what, monks, is impermanent? Form, monks, is impermanent … Feeling … Perception ……
content: “Monks, whatever is impermanent, you should abandon your desire for it. And what, monks, is impermanent? Form, monks, is impermanent … Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is impermanent — there you should abandon your desire. Whatever is impermanent, monks, there you should abandon your desire.”

title: Māra: You are young and beautiful, I am young and in my prime. With the five-tuned lute, Enjoy yourself, Khemā. Elder Nun Khemā: With this…
content:
Māra:

You are young and beautiful,
I am young and in my prime.
With the five-tuned lute,
Enjoy yourself, Khemā.

Elder Nun Khemā:

With this foul body,
Diseased and fragile —
I am disenchanted, disgusted.
Sensual desire has been uprooted.

Sensual desires are like swords and spears —
The aggregates are a chopping block.
What you call sensual pleasure —
I have now abandoned it.

Everywhere, delight is destroyed,
The mass of delusion is shattered.
Know this, O Evil One —
You are defeated, Māra.

You worship the stars!
You worship fire in the deep forest —
You do not know the truth —
Fools think it is pure.

But I pay homage
To the Awakened One, the Supreme Man,
Who has escaped all suffering,
Following the Teacher’s instruction.

title: “Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is…
content: “Once, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down and seized a quail. Then, monks, the quail, while being carried off by the hawk, lamented: ‘This is my misfortune! This is my lack of merit! For I wandered outside my own proper range, into the domain of others. If I had kept to my own proper range, my ancestral territory, this hawk would not have been a match for me in battle.’ - ‘What, quail, is your own proper range, your ancestral territory?’ - ‘A field plowed with a plow.’ Then, monks, the hawk, not boasting of its own strength, not pressing its own strength, released the quail and said: ‘Go, quail. Even after going there, I will not let you go.’ Then, monks, the quail went to a field plowed with a plow, climbed onto a large clod of earth, stood on it, and said to the hawk: ‘Come at me, hawk! Come at me, hawk!’ Then the hawk, boasting of its own strength, pressing its own strength, folding both wings, suddenly swooped down on the quail. When the quail knew: ‘This hawk is swooping down hard on me,’ it hid behind that clod of earth. Then, monks, the hawk shattered its own breast. So too, monks, for one who wanders outside his own proper range, into the domain of others. Therefore, monks, do not wander outside your own proper range, into the domain of others. For one who wanders outside his proper range, into the domain of others, Māra gains an opportunity, Māra gains an object.”

title: Sitting down to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One: - Here, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala has had many people bound.…
content:
Sitting down to one side, those monks said to the Blessed One:
- Here, venerable sir, King Pasenadi of Kosala has had many people bound. Some are bound with ropes, some with chains, some with shackles.

Then the Blessed One, understanding the meaning of this, on that occasion recited this verse:
The wise say that such binding
Is not strong —
Binding with iron, with ropes,
With wooden shackles —
But infatuation with sensual pleasures,
With jewels and ornaments,
And anxious thoughts
Directed toward children and wives —
The wise say this binding
Is truly strong.
Though it drags one down,
Subtle and hard to escape,
True renunciants cut it in two,
Without wishing or longing,
Abandoning all sensual pleasures.

title: “Monks, I am freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, you too are freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, wander…
content: “Monks, I am freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, you too are freed from all traps, both heavenly and human. Monks, wander for the happiness of the many, for the welfare of the many, out of compassion for the world, for the benefit, happiness, and welfare of gods and humans. Do not go two by the same road. Monks, teach the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing. Proclaim the holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. There are beings with little dust in their eyes who, if they do not hear the Dhamma, will decline. They will become those who understand the Dhamma. Monks, I will go to Uruvelā, the town of Senā, to teach the Dhamma.”

title: “Monks, sensual thought is blind, causes blindness, causes lack of knowledge, leads to the destruction of wisdom, partakes of distress, does not lead to Nibbāna.…
content:
“Monks, sensual thought is blind, causes blindness, causes lack of knowledge, leads to the destruction of wisdom, partakes of distress, does not lead to Nibbāna. Monks, ill-will thought is blind … harmful thought is blind, causes blindness, causes lack of knowledge, leads to the destruction of wisdom, partakes of distress, does not lead to Nibbāna.

Three thoughts of wholesome kind
One should frequently reflect upon —
Three unwholesome thoughts should be abandoned, turned away from.
That one surely restrains
The conduct of thoughts.

As rain settles the dust,
So by calming thoughts with the mind,
One here and now attains
The peaceful path of peace.”

title: “Venerable sir, ‘stain’ is called a stain. What term is synonymous with what is called ‘stain’?” “Venerable sir, evil, unwholesome states, the realm of sensual…
content:
“Venerable sir, ‘stain’ is called a stain. What term is synonymous with what is called ‘stain’?”
“Venerable sir, evil, unwholesome states, the realm of sensual desire, are synonymous with what is called ‘stain.’”

title: “Monks, what is non-clinging and non-worry? Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple regards form as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is…
content: “Monks, what is non-clinging and non-worry? Here, monks, a well-taught noble disciple regards form as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ For him, that form changes and alters. When form changes and alters, no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair arise in him. He regards feeling … perception … formations … consciousness as: ‘This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.’ For him, that consciousness changes and alters. When consciousness changes and alters, no sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or despair arise in him. Thus, monks, is non-clinging and non-worry.”
